item.title: AI focus shifts to application and regulation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
AI focus shifts to application and regulation China's approach to generative artificial intelligence is evolving from a focus solely on technological development to emphasizing both practical application and comprehensive regulation, according to a new report. Over the past year, China has been refining its policies on generative AI, which refers to AI systems that can produce original content such as text, images, music and videos, advancing on two fronts: technological application and risk management. This is highlighted in a report released on Tuesday by the policy and international cooperation division of the China Internet Network Information Center. Wang Changqing, head of the division, underscored while introducing the report the importance of balancing AI development with governance, noting that Chinese authorities have formulated around 20 regulations related to AI since June 2025, as AI use in China rapidly grows. As of June, the number of generative AI users in China had surpassed 700 million, an increase of 98 million since December 2025. Approximately 76 percent of internet users primarily engage with AI for question-and-answer purposes, followed by tasks such as processing images, videos and text and creating meeting summaries, according to the report. The report also indicates that China is home to 10,740 companies involved in AI large models, AI agents, robotics and related fields, with the technology being widely applied across various sectors, including agriculture, industrial manufacturing, programming, office work, embodied intelligence and scientific research. To maximize the technological value and regulate the use of AI, Wang noted that several authorities, including the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Commerce and the National Health Commission, have developed guidelines for integrating AI into their respective sectors. For example, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued guidelines on merging AI with communications to bolster the infrastructure for AI development. Additionally, the report stresses the need to uphold security standards, showing that a series of rules have been established and improved to address issues such as ethical risks of AI and enhancement of protection for minors. Shen Juncheng, an employee of general AI technology company MiniMax, praised these measures for their positive impact on real-world application and security governance. "The policy environment encourages technological advancement while equally emphasizing development and governance," he said. Zheng Ning, head of the law department at Communication University of China's School of Cultural Industries Management, said it is crucial to balance technological application with risk prevention and control. "Unlocking AI's industrial value is about technological application, while regulatory governance ensures security. They are two sides of the same coin, not mutually exclusive," she said. Initially, the primary challenge was addressing technological weaknesses, so policies focused on breakthroughs, Zheng added. "As AI enters widespread application, the risk of misuse becomes more prominent. Thus, policies have shifted to focus on 'how to use it and how to govern it'. Technological breakthroughs remain essential, but they are no longer the sole focus," she said. While commending the advancements in AI-related policies aimed at fostering healthy technological development, Zheng called for greater efforts in crafting regulations that enhance oversight and clarify the responsibilities of stakeholders in the AI industry — including developers, operators and users — to create a cohesive framework for AI governance. She also advocated effective policymaking to tackle challenges posed by AI deepfakes and to protect children from harmful AI-generated content. caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Six major contributors call for EU budget cut
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Six major contributors call for EU budget cut Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is leading a group of six countries threatening to withhold their backing for the European Union's next seven-year budget unless substantial cuts are made, highlighting divisions within the 27-nation bloc over where its focus should be. The proposed budget for the years 2028 to 2034, which is worth 2 trillion euros ($2.3 trillion), must have unanimous backing to be adopted, but the Financial Times newspaper has seen a letter signed by Merz and by the heads of government of Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden — countries that together make up nearly 40 percent of EU budget revenue — demanding changes. The situation is all the more delicate because of pressure to agree a budget before next year, when there will be a presidential election in France, and general elections in Italy, Poland, and Spain, all of which could potentially have a huge impact on the political tone and direction of national and supranational politics. Merz has said that a "20th century budget" cannot address contemporary challenges, and the letter says it "must be fundamentally reformed. We must make choices". It is believed that the signatories' alternative vision of Europe's financial future would see less spent on agriculture and support for poorer regions of the bloc, which absorb much of its resources, and more devoted to challenges including security and global trade. "Our six countries alone finance almost 40 percent of all member states' contributions," the letter says. "While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden." Differing national priorities are being highlighted by the split, and it falls to Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, to come up with a compromise by the middle of next month, which will be a huge challenge because of fundamental differences of opinion between countries. Most countries oppose the German-backed reduction on spending in areas including agriculture, saying that spending should instead be increased, which is something the signatories have rejected as "simply not realistic". Some nations have proposed that the EU should borrow more, which is anathema to Germany and its supporters. Earlier this month, Merz said "excessive debt threatens our sovereignty and our capacity to act", and that governments have the "admittedly painful task" of setting priorities. Despite European Council President Antonio Costa being publicly upbeat about the chances of common ground being found, the Politico website has seen German diplomatic messages saying that "no potential areas for compromise were apparent" when the two sides had negotiations earlier this month, and referring to attitudes on both sides of the dispute as being "entrenched positions". julian@mail.chinadailyuk.com

item.title: Imports poised to hit record high
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Imports poised to hit record high Jan-Aug incoming goods surged to 14.61 trln yuan, strongest growth since 2021 China's imports are on track to reach a new high this year, as its evolving market and continued opening-up generate more orders for foreign firms and broader opportunities across global supply chains, said commerce officials. The country's imports rose 22 percent year-on-year to 14.61 trillion yuan ($2.18 trillion) in the first eight months, the strongest January-August growth since 2021, the Ministry of Commerce said. Yang Tao, director-general of the ministry's department of foreign trade, said the strong growth comes as China steps up efforts to expand imports through policy support and trade promotion activities. These efforts are giving foreign enterprises greater access to the country's vast consumer market and industrial demand. Zhang Li, assistant minister of commerce, said the country has held the China International Import Expo for eight consecutive years and launched the "Big Market for All: Export to China" campaign, creating more channels and platforms for high-quality products from around the world to enter its market. As more high-quality foreign products reach China's consumer market and become part of its industrial and supply chains, Zhang said the benefits of the country's import growth are extending beyond overseas exporters alone. This growth is generating new orders across related industries and supporting job creation in their home markets. Chen Jianwei, a researcher specializing in foreign trade at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said the acceleration in imports reflects not only stronger consumer demand, but also increased purchases by China's production sector as manufacturers secure raw materials, intermediate goods and equipment for future output. Sustained growth in imports of production inputs can indicate manufacturers' confidence in future domestic and overseas demand, Chen said. Ningbo Lingyue Intelligent Equipment Co Ltd, a lawn mower manufacturer in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, imported more than 60 million yuan worth of gasoline engines, axles, clutches and other key components from the United States during the January-August period, according to Ningbo Customs. Zhang Enhui, the company's operations director, said the US remains both the company's largest source of imports and its biggest export market. Components sourced from the US account for more than 60 percent of its total imports, while sales to the US represent more than half of its exports. "The recent tariff reductions announced by the US government will also benefit our exports, giving us greater confidence to increase research and development investment in response to overseas customer demand, and further expand our presence in the US market," said Zhang Enhui. Import growth is not confined to industrial inputs, with growing consumer demand and more efficient customs clearance bringing a wider range of fresh foods and other high-quality products to Chinese consumers. Between January and August, customs authorities at Nanjing Lukou International Airport in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, facilitated the clearance of 3,408 metric tons of imported fresh produce and seafood, including Norwegian salmon, tree-ripened durians from Malaysia, mud crabs from Bangladesh, and fresh peaches and plums from Australia, up 144 percent year-on-year. Guan Lixin, a researcher specializing in marketing and consumption at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing, said China's consumption upgrading is creating new opportunities for foreign companies as demand shifts toward higher-quality, more diverse and specialized goods. For foreign firms, this shift provides greater room to introduce premium products, tailor offerings to Chinese consumers, and invest more in innovation and local market development, said Guan. zhongnan@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Chinese county plucks strings of global violin market
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
When Gao Yanding decided to make his own violin, he started with an unusual piece of wood: spruce that had been naturally aged for three decades. The Chinese-American scientist, who spent more than 20 years conducting biomedical engineering research in the United States, wanted to answer a question that had fascinated him for years as an amateur violinist. Why can two instruments made from seemingly similar pieces of wood produce vastly different sounds — and command dramatically different prices? To find the answer, Gao brought the carefully selected tonewood to Queshan county in Zhumadian, Central China's Henan province. There, he worked with veteran luthier Jiang Baoming to build a violin and applied scientific methods to analyze and refine its acoustics. Through their collaboration, Gao acquired nine violins from Jiang, each of which saw its value increase significantly. His experiment reflects a much larger transformation taking place in Queshan, an agricultural county that has become one of the world's largest violin manufacturing centers. Today, the county produces around 400,000 violins annually, supplying customers across Europe, North America and Asia. Local industry officials said Queshan has become China's leading production base for mid — to high-end handmade violins, producing more than 80 percent of the country's total. The industry's roots in Queshan date back to the 1980s, when several craftsmen traveled to Beijing to learn violin making before returning to establish workshops. One of them was Wang Jinwu. Now 54, Wang has spent four decades making violins. Wang's workshop has built long-term relationships with overseas buyers, including a United States musical instrument wholesaler that has worked with him for nearly two decades. The partnership began when the buyer discovered Wang's violins at an international trade fair, purchased one instrument, and later placed an initial order for 10 violins. As trust grew, so did the business. Today, the customer buys more than 2,000 violins from Wang each year. "Overseas customers value Queshan violins because they are handmade, reliable in quality and reasonably priced," Wang said. According to local authorities, Queshan now has 144 violin-related companies employing more than 2,600 people. Together, they generate annual revenues of more than 600 million yuan ($89.4 million), supported by a complete supply chain covering wood processing, component manufacturing, varnishing, assembly and packaging. The concentration of suppliers and skilled workers has helped lower production costs while allowing manufacturers to develop more specialized production processes. Rather than training every apprentice to master the entire violin-making process, local producers have increasingly adopted a division-of-labor model. "In the past, it took about three years to train someone to make a complete violin," Wang said. "Today, workers can become production-ready in around three months by specializing in just one stage of the process." The next challenge for Queshan's violin makers is expanding their reach beyond traditional export channels. For years, most instruments were sold overseas through distributors. Increasingly, manufacturers are turning to cross-border e-commerce platforms, short videos and livestreaming to connect directly with international buyers. "Professional buyers have long known that many high-quality handmade violins come from Queshan," said Jiang Baolin, secretary-general of the Queshan Handmade Violin Makers Association. "The difference now is that overseas consumers have more direct access to buying them." To sustain the industry's growth, local players are also focusing on cultivating younger generations of people involved in the craft. "We hope the next generation will inherit not only the skills, but also the artistry behind the craft," Jiang said. WANG ZHUOQIONG in Zhumadian, Henan

item.title: Autumn harvest underway after record summer crop
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Autumn harvest underway after record summer crop Strong yields come as nation seeks to buffer food security amid intl volatility China's summer grain output topped 150 million metric tons for the first time this year, while the autumn grain harvest is underway and the full-year crop is on track for another bumper harvest, Agriculture and Rural Affairs Minister Zhang Zhu said on Tuesday. With early rice production remaining above 28 million tons for six consecutive years, attention is now turning to autumn grain, which accounts for about three-quarters of the country's annual grain output, Zhang said. More than 20 percent of the autumn grain area has already been harvested, while the planted area is expected to remain stable or increase slightly from last year. Corn, a major feed grain, has seen a particularly notable increase in planted area, Zhang said. "If weather conditions remain generally normal in the later stages, we are likely to see another bumper harvest," Zhang said. China has experienced more flooding than drought this year, although the impacts have generally been more severe in localized areas. Overall, weather conditions have been favorable for agricultural production, he said. The strong harvest comes as global grain markets face greater volatility and China seeks to strengthen food security during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30). Grain supply and demand will remain "tightly balanced" during the period, Zhang said. While consumption of staple grains such as rice and wheat is declining, rising demand for meat, eggs and dairy products is increasing demand for feed grains such as corn and soybeans, he added. "Overall grain demand will continue to rise, and the string of food security should always be tightly wound," he said. China also needs to adjust the structure of its grain supply, Zhang said, noting that the country still relies heavily on imported soybeans for edible oil and animal feed. At the same time, supplies of high-quality grain products need to increase. These include specialized strong- and weak-gluten wheat used to make bread and cakes, as well as better-tasting premium rice varieties. The ministry will implement a new round of measures to raise grain production capacity, targeting about 725 million tons by the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan period. "Increasing yields is the key to these measures," Zhang said. Yield increases accounted for more than 60 percent of grain production growth during the 14th Five-Year Plan period and more than 90 percent last year. The ministry will promote the integrated use of better farmland, improved seeds, machinery and farming practices to raise yields across larger areas, Zhang said. It will also optimize the mix of agricultural products, maintaining stable staple grain output while increasing corn and soybean production and expanding sources of edible oils. Beyond cropland, China plans to diversify its food supply as consumer diets change, Chen Bangxun, a ministry spokesman, said. Modern greenhouses can annually produce five to eight times as many vegetables per hectare as open fields. The ministry will expand efficient greenhouse farming to make food supplies less dependent on seasons and weather. "China will also make greater use of rivers, lakes and oceans," Chen said. Large and smart deep-sea aquaculture cages can produce up to 1,000 tons of large yellow croaker a year, providing high-quality aquatic products. The country will also explore synthetic biology to develop new protein sources and food products, he added. zhaoyimeng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Lines perfected: Divine strokes of Yongle Palace
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Place a Chinese mural next to a Western one, and the Chinese mural's line work stands out immediately. Alina Efimova, a cultural observer from Russia with a deep interest in Chinese murals, sat down with Dong Zhuo, vice-dean of the School of Restoration at the Central Academy of Fine Arts, to explore just how remarkable this line art really is. How many types of brushstrokes are there in Chinese painting? How do painters convey different textures using only changes in lines? And how was the three-meter-long line in the Yongle Palace murals drawn in one smooth, unbroken stroke? Follow their conversation to find out the secret behind these lines. Into Chinese Art is an immersive cultural interview series produced by China Daily Culture Channel, where international hosts engage with art experts through interactive discussions, offering audiences a deeper understanding of Chinese art and aesthetics. The fourth season of the series focuses on murals. Related:

item.title: Shanxi a good model for energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
UK ambassador: Shanxi a good model for energy transition Share - WeChat
After first visiting Shanxi 30 years ago, Peter Wilson CMG, the British Ambassador to China, returned with one striking observation: the air is better. He sees Shanxi's ambitious shift from coal to new-energy sources as a transformation improving local lives while offering valuable lessons for the world. Importantly, he views UK-China cooperation not as a one-way transfer of experience, but as an opportunity to learn from both successes and failures. From coal transition to green technologies, Shanxi offers a revealing window into China's energy transformation. Reporters: Zhu Xingxin, Liu Jianna

item.title: Coo the music, pigeons set city's tone
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Coo the music, pigeons set city's tone Beijing breeders keep tradition of whistling wings, ornamental and racing birds alive In his 1934 essay Autumn in Peiping, writer Yu Dafu described sitting in a courtyard on an autumn morning, looking up at the blue sky and hearing "the sound of domesticated pigeons flying overhead" — part of the unhurried, peaceful rhythm of everyday life in Beijing. Nearly a century later, pigeons are still a defining characteristic of some areas of the city's skyline. On Sept 21, Chinese and foreign guests released white pigeons at a gathering to mark the International Day of Peace. The birds, rising together above the crowd, were a familiar symbol of peace. Similar scenes have unfolded at Tian'anmen Square during National Day celebrations and other major commemorations, when thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of pigeons have been released above the heart of Beijing. But behind the feathered pageantry is a community with lifelong passion for pigeons and associated traditions. Some of the pigeons released on Sept 21 were raised and trained by Li Xiaolong, a veteran pigeon-keeper from Xicheng district. Li has been around pigeons since he was 3 years old. "I'd hold a pigeon in my hands and play with it," he said. "I was at the pigeon loft almost every day." His love of the birds drew another Beijing boy into the world of pigeons. Ma Chunyu was not yet in kindergarten when he got his first pair of pigeons, taken from beneath the eaves of a neighbor's house. By primary school, his obsession had become difficult for his family to control. "I would secretly take a pigeon to school," Ma recalled. "I'd hide it in my schoolbag, then reach into the book compartment and take it out to stroke it." His mother worried that the birds were keeping him from his homework. Once, when she grabbed a broom and went after his pigeons, Ma wrapped himself around her legs to stop her. When Ma was about 9, he became interested in racing pigeons, which involves training them to return to their home loft from a distant location. "We started at 5 kilometers, then 10 km, and just kept going farther," he said. As a teenager, Ma carried dozens of pigeons in wooden crates, first by bicycle and then by long-distance bus, sometimes traveling more than 80 km before releasing them. "The pigeons got back first — of course they did," he said. "But it took me about two hours." More than half a century later, Ma still keeps pigeons. "When you're upset, you look at them cooing around you, almost like they're talking to you," he said. "Once you see the pigeons, there are no worries." There are fewer places in Beijing today where pigeons can be kept than when Ma was a child. Many courtyard homes and low-rise neighborhoods once suited to pigeon lofts have disappeared or changed. Keeping birds in densely populated residential communities also raises concerns over space, sanitation and disturbance to neighbors. Some longtime pigeon-keepers have moved their birds far from the city center or changed how they raise them, however, several of them told China Daily they now see relatively few young people taking up the pastime.

From mountain terraces to ancient landmarks and island waters, these five destinations offer inspiration for a National Day holiday getaway, boasting fine mild autumn conditions in early October. Bijie, Guizhou — Music among the terraces In Bijie's Dafang county, the curved terraces of Shexiang Ancient Town resemble a giant fingerprint. The landscape has also become a setting for open-air concerts, with lights tracing the terraces as music fills the night.
